b: CHICAGO — Every marketer knows the value of social media — and every successful marketer knows that social media marketing changes every day.

To keep you on the cutting edge, Trade Show Executive’s Young Professionals Corner connected with Sara Fellows, Group Director, Communications at mdg, a major force in the association and event marketing space.
Fellows leads the organization’s social media department and helps grow its services, position its team as trendsetters and deliver innovative strategies for its clients.
Get her expert perspectives on social media marketing below!

“What excites me most is the opportunity for trade shows to use social media as a source of business intelligence, not just a marketing channel,” Fellows said. “Social is shaping our culture in real time, and there’s so much valuable information available about what our audiences care about, the challenges they’re facing and the conversations happening across their industries.

“Imagine using social listening to identify emerging industry trends and letting those insights help inform conference tracks and programming, or tapping into online communities to get real-time feedback during the planning process. We can use social to better understand what’s important to our audiences and then translate that information into more relevant and meaningful event experiences.”

Fellows added that there’s also a huge opportunity to think about events through the lens of shareability. She explained that when organizers intentionally create experiences that people want to capture and share, attendees become advocates, extending an event’s reach far beyond the show floor and generating earned exposure in the process.
Social Media Do’s and Don’ts for 2027
Sara Fellows, Group Director, Communications at mdg
Fellows provided these social media do’s and don’ts for the year ahead.

Lead with audience value: “Start with a hook that speaks to something your audience is interested in, then connect it back to your event. Whether it’s an industry trend, a common challenge or a timely conversation, give people a reason to pay attention before introducing the promotional message.”

Put people at the center of your content: “Your own team, speakers, exhibitors, attendees and industry experts are some of your greatest content resources. Give them opportunities to share their perspectives and expertise. People connect with people, even in B2B.”

Build a year-round content strategy: “Industry conversations don’t stop when your event ends, and neither should your social presence. Create content that provides value between show cycles and gives your community reasons to stay engaged (and loyal).”

Rely too heavily on promotional content: “Registration deadlines, speaker announcements and event updates are important, but there’s an opportunity to balance them with content that educates, entertains and inspires your audience.”

Measure success by registrations alone: “Social plays a role throughout the attendee journey, from awareness and discovery to consideration and ultimately attendance. Look at the full picture to understand how your content is contributing to your event’s goals.”

Be afraid to experiment: “B2B audiences appreciate humor, personality and creativity just as much as anyone else. Explore social-first formats and emerging trends that make sense for your audience and industry.”

“We’re already seeing organizers doing some really innovative things in this space, and I think we’re at an exciting turning point for the industry. The more we bring social insights into our business decisions, the more opportunities we have to create events that feel relevant and exciting,” Fellows said.
How is Social Media Marketing Changing?

“I think the biggest shift we’re seeing is in how people use social media,” Fellows said. “It’s evolved far beyond a place to connect with friends and family. People are increasingly turning to these platforms to discover new things, learn about what’s happening in the world and make decisions.”

Fellows added that Reuters Institute’s 2026 Digital News Report found that 54% of people across the markets surveyed now use social media and video networks for news, surpassing traditional news websites and apps for the first time, and, according to DataReportal, 41.8% of online adults use social networks to research brands and evaluate potential purchases.

“For marketers, this represents a fundamental shift in how we need to think about social,” Fellows explained. “It’s not just a place to distribute marketing messages anymore. It’s where people are learning, forming opinions and deciding what’s worth their time and attention. For trade show organizers, the opportunity is significant. Our audiences are already using these platforms to discover information and engage with their industries. The question is how we can become a valuable part of those conversations.”
Social media algorithms are completely reshaping the way Fellows thinks about content creation and audience growth.

“Historically, you’d post something to your social channel and it would primarily be shown to your followers,” Fellows said. “Today, platforms are delivering content based on individual interests, meaning two people could follow (or not even follow and still receive) the exact same account but see completely different content from it.”

Fellows explained that these algorithms are getting more sophisticated every day. For example, TikTok has confirmed that follower count isn’t a direct factor in how its “For You” feed recommends content.

“That fundamentally changes how we should think about success,” Fellows said. “Having a large following is great, but it’s no longer the best indicator of how many people your content can reach. The metrics that matter are evolving, too. Likes used to be a primary measure of engagement, but platforms are increasingly looking at signals like watch time and shares to determine what content deserves broader distribution. Instagram, for example, has identified watch time, likes and sends as its three most important ranking signals, with sends playing a particularly important role in reaching people who don’t already follow you.”

Fellows said that for event organizers, this creates both an opportunity and a challenge: Your content has the potential to reach entirely new audiences, but only if it’s relevant and engaging enough to earn their attention.

“It also means having a team that understands how platforms are evolving, knows what metrics actually matter and can connect content performance back to the event’s larger business objectives is more important than ever,” Fellows said.
According to Fellows, some of the biggest challenges facing social media marketers are:

Resources: “Social media has become increasingly complex, but the resources allocated to it haven’t necessarily kept pace. Teams are expected to understand constantly changing algorithms, manage multiple platforms, create more sophisticated content and deliver bigger results, often without additional support. It’s becoming harder to treat social as something someone can just manage on the side of their other responsibilities.”

Measurement: “Organizers understandably want to know how social contributes to attendance, but there’s often too much emphasis on direct registrations or traditional metrics like follower growth. Social plays a role throughout the attendee journey, from introducing someone to an event for the first time to building enough interest and credibility that they eventually decide to attend. Measuring that influence requires looking at more than just the last click.”

Access to Content: “Trade shows are full of incredible stories, industry experts and interesting conversations, but social teams don’t always have easy access to them. Some of the best content opportunities already exist within an event’s community. The challenge is creating the relationships and processes needed to consistently turn those opportunities into compelling content.”
Fellows generously provided FAQs to help event professionals with social media marketing.
Q: What should be avoided at all costs? What are some horizons that are worth exploring?

A: I’d avoid treating social media as something that can simply be added to someone’s existing responsibilities without the right time, resources or expertise. Social has evolved so much beyond scheduling posts, and building an effective strategy requires a deep understanding of audience behavior, platform algorithms, content creation and measurement.

I’d also avoid assuming that content created for other marketing channels will automatically work on social. An email campaign and an Instagram Reel serve very different purposes. That doesn’t mean you can’t repurpose content, but you need to think about how to adapt the message and format to what people actually want to consume on each platform.
As far as opportunities worth exploring, I’d love to see more B2B event marketers borrow from the B2C playbook. At mdg, we have a saying: “We’re marketing to people.”

Freeman’s latest Trends Report found that about half of attendees either pay their own way or initiate the decision to attend and make the case to their employer. That makes reaching and influencing individuals more important than ever.

At the end of the day, we’re showing up in someone’s feed alongside content from their friends and family, favorite creators and consumer brands. We’re all competing for the same attention, and that means we need to think about what makes content interesting and worth engaging with. There’s so much opportunity to bring more personality, creativity and social-first storytelling into how we market trade shows.
Q: How often should we post?

A: A good general rule of thumb is three to five times per week. Quality matters more than quantity, but consistency over time is also important. Avoid going dark for months between events. Social media should be an ongoing conversation with your audience, not something you turn on and off as registration opens and closes.
Q: Which social media platforms should we be on?

A: For most events, LinkedIn, Instagram and Facebook are the core platforms to prioritize. TikTok, Threads and Bluesky are worth exploring depending on your audience. We’re also seeing growing interest in Reddit, where a more grassroots, community-first approach can help events participate in existing industry conversations.
Q: Which metrics should we be tracking?

A: Engagement rate is one of the most useful indicators of how well your content resonates. Look beyond likes to comments, shares and saves, which can tell you more about what your audience finds valuable. Reach and impressions are also important for understanding awareness, while website traffic and registrations can help connect social activity to event goals.
Q: Does responding to comments actually make a difference?

A: Absolutely! Social media is meant to be social. A 2026 Buffer study found that posts where brands and creators responded to comments saw 30% higher engagement on LinkedIn, 21% on Instagram and 9% more reactions on Facebook. While this doesn’t prove that responding directly causes the increase, it makes a strong case for treating community management as part of your social strategy, not an afterthought.
Q: Does the time of day we post matter?

A: Yes, but increasingly less than you might think. Social algorithms prioritize relevance and engagement, meaning great content can continue reaching audiences well after it’s published. Rather than relying on generic “best times to post” recommendations, use your own audience data to identify when your followers are most active and adjust from there.

A: Not nearly as much as they used to! In fact, recent research found that Instagram posts using hashtags averaged 32% fewer views and 34% fewer interactions (Metricool’s 2026 Instagram Study) than the platform average. Social platforms are increasingly functioning like search engines, so keywords in your captions, on-screen text and video content are becoming much more important for discoverability.
Hashtags still have a place, particularly branded event hashtags that help connect conversations, but they’re no longer the growth tactic they once were.
Fellows also provided common social media marketing myths — and the truth behind them.
Myth: Every post should promote registration.

Truth: Social media isn’t just another advertising channel. If every post is asking someone to register, you’re missing the opportunity to build interest, demonstrate value and create a community around your event. Promotional content absolutely has a place, but it should be balanced with content your audience genuinely wants to consume.
Myth: Our logo needs to be front and center on every post.

Truth: Your event’s brand is much more than its logo. Consistent visuals, tone of voice and content can build recognition without needing to put your logo on every asset. Content that feels native to the platform is often more engaging than something that looks like an advertisement. The goal is to make people stop scrolling, not immediately recognize that they’re being marketed to.
Myth: You can throw together a social media post in 20 minutes.

Truth: Sure, you can publish something in 20 minutes, but creating content that actually performs takes more thought. From researching what your audience cares about to developing the concept, creating visuals, writing copy and optimizing for each platform, there’s a lot happening behind the scenes. Great social content doesn’t happen by accident, and treating it as an afterthought rarely delivers results.
Myth: B2B social media has to be serious and professional.

Truth: There’s a balance. You’re still representing your brand, but social media is also a place to show personality and relatability. That starts with understanding your audience’s “pop culture DNA,” the trends, humor, entertainment and cultural references they connect with. You don’t have to jump on every trend, but finding ways to connect your industry to the broader culture can make your content feel more relevant and engaging without sacrificing credibility.
Myth: Onsite social is just posting show-floor photos.

Truth: Onsite social should be an extension of the event experience. It’s an opportunity to capture real conversations, showcase the people behind the industry, help attendees navigate the show and create FOMO for those who aren’t there. Think storytelling, not just documentation.
